title: Schizophrenia is a Disorder of Developmental Synaptic Selection
content: Schizophrenia is strongly heritable, yet psychosis usually becomes clinically apparent during adolescence or early adulthood, when cortical circuits remain under active refinement. This theory addresses that developmental timing by distinguishing moment-to-moment neural activity from durable biological change. At the encoding layer, the ARCH × Φ framework represents effective neural writing as Wₙ = Aₙ × Dₙ × Cₙ × Φₙ. Aₙ denotes the neural machinery available for modification, Dₙ the strength of the modification signal, Cₙ the context that determines which representation is selected, and Φₙ the permissive state that allows selected activity to produce lasting change. Wₙ therefore represents the degree to which a current neural event becomes durably incorporated into molecular, synaptic, or circuit structure. The model proposes that schizophrenia can arise when adolescent development repeatedly selects the wrong substrate, fails to stabilize the right substrate, or allows elimination to outpace stabilization. Filial imprinting provides an experimental precedent because mTORC1 blockade prevents experience-dependent mushroom-spine stabilization while thin-spine loss continues. Schizophrenia research independently implicates complement-associated synaptic elimination, altered AMPA-receptor trafficking, dopamine-mediated aberrant salience, reduced physiological plasticity, atypical chromatin accessibility, inhibitory-circuit abnormalities, and altered AKT–mTORC1 signaling. These mechanisms occupy different positions within the same framework rather than serving as competing explanations. Because the modified substrate becomes the architecture for subsequent cognition, developmental selection becomes recursive. The theory predicts that longitudinal measures of synaptic stabilization and elimination during adolescence will be more informative than static measures of synaptic density alone.
